title: Smoothness of time functions and the metric splitting of globally hyperbolic spacetimes
version: arXiv gr-qc/0401112v3 (15 Feb 2005); Commun. Math. Phys. 257 (2005), 43–50
relevance: Sharp existence result linking global hyperbolicity to a smooth Cauchy temporal function and orthogonal product splitting.
locators: Abstract; Sec. 1, Theorems 1.1–1.2; proof construction Secs. 2–3, especially Prop. 2.4 and Theorem 3.11.
assumptions: Time-oriented smooth Lorentzian spacetime; Theorem 1.1 assumes global hyperbolicity. Theorem 1.2 assumes an existing continuous time function.
conclusion: Authors prove every globally hyperbolic spacetime admits a smooth function with timelike gradient whose levels are spacelike Cauchy hypersurfaces, yielding a smooth splitting M ≅ R × S and metric form −β dT² + g_T. Any spacetime admitting a time function admits a temporal function. The theorem supplies existence, not a unique or physically preferred foliation.
proof_status: Published mathematical proof read in the arXiv HTML; not independently reproduced.
dependencies: Bernal and Sánchez 2003, arXiv:gr-qc/0306108v2; Geroch 1970, cited in the paper
open_questions: What additional physical structure, if any, selects one among the admissible Cauchy temporal functions? This paper does not answer that interpretive question.
limits: Mathematical existence theorem only; it does not imply objective passage, determinism, or a temporal ontology.

title: On smooth Cauchy hypersurfaces and Geroch’s splitting theorem
relevance: Smooths Geroch’s topological splitting result under global hyperbolicity.
locators: Abstract; Sec. 1, Theorem 1.1; Sec. 2, Remark 2.3; Sec. 4 proof of Theorem 1.1 (lines 254 onward in arXiv HTML).
assumptions: Globally hyperbolic spacetime; the result concerns existence of a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface and product diffeomorphism.
conclusion: Authors prove existence of a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface S₀ and M diffeomorphic to R × S₀. Remark 2.3 warns that constant-s slices in the preliminary splitting are not necessarily Cauchy; do not infer that every product coordinate supplies a Cauchy foliation.
proof_status: Published mathematical proof read in the arXiv HTML; not independently reproduced.
dependencies: Geroch 1970, as summarized and used in the paper
open_questions: The paper gives existence, not preferred-slicing selection.
limits: Topological/smooth splitting result; no claim about temporal ontology or passage.

title: The Cosmological Time Function
version: arXiv gr-qc/9709084v1 (30 Sep 1997); Class. Quantum Grav. 15 (1998), 309–322
relevance: Defines cosmological time from Lorentzian distance and proves strong consequences under a regularity condition.
locators: Definition 1.1 and Theorem 1.2, pp. 1–2 (PDF); Corollary 2.6, p. 9 (levels are future Cauchy); Abstract, p. 1.
assumptions: Time-oriented Lorentzian manifold; τ(q)=sup_{p<q} d(p,q) must be finite everywhere and tend to zero on every past-inextendible causal curve. The paper notes Minkowski space has τ identically infinite (p. 1).
conclusion: Authors prove regular cosmological time implies global hyperbolicity and that τ is a continuous, strictly increasing time function, locally Lipschitz (second derivatives a.e.); its nonempty levels are future Cauchy surfaces, not thereby two-sided Cauchy or smooth leaves.
proof_status: Primary PDF opened; abstract, definition and theorem/corollary statements checked; full proof not audited.
open_questions: The physical adequacy of the regularity hypothesis and which cosmological models satisfy it are model-specific questions.
limits: Partial source reading. Cosmological time is canonically defined from the metric once the regularity premises hold, but that fact alone does not establish a preferred physical slicing or an ontology. Avoid the earlier salvage note’s unsupported blanket claim that de Sitter is excluded; only the Minkowski example was directly checked here.

title: An Example of a New Type of Cosmological Solutions of Einstein’s Field Equations of Gravitation
relevance: Original rotating cosmological solution demonstrates a time-oriented spacetime with closed timelike curves and without a global time coordinate strictly increasing along every future timelike direction.
locators: Properties (4)–(6), p. 448 (PDF); derivation of property (6), pp. 449–450 (PDF), including timelike circles at sufficiently large radius and closed timelike lines.
assumptions: Gödel’s exact homogeneous rotating dust solution of Einstein’s field equations with the paper’s stated cosmological constant/matter setup.
conclusion: The author states that a consistent local time orientation exists (property 4), while no global time coordinate increases along every positive timelike direction (property 5); closed timelike lines exist (property 6). Thus chronology violation is compatible with local time orientation. Closed timelike curves preclude a time function and global hyperbolicity by standard causal implications; that latter implication is a mathematical inference, not a separate theorem stated in this paper.
proof_status: Original four-page primary article read; its property statements and displayed metric argument for closed timelike lines checked. No independent derivation of the full solution.
dependencies: The specific Gödel solution and metric argument given in the source
open_questions: The example is an exact solution, not a claim that such a spacetime is physically realized.
limits: A counterexample to unrestricted global-time conclusions from Einstein’s equations alone; does not settle chronology protection or the global status of all physically admissible spacetimes.

title: Canonical Quantum Gravity and the Problem of Time
version: arXiv gr-qc/9210011v1 (submitted 21 Oct 1992), Part 1 of the lecture write-up; HTML v1
relevance: Classic review of canonical GR and approaches to the problem of time, including the foliation setup, Dirac constraint quantization, internal time, and global/multiple-choice problems.
locators: Secs. 2.2–2.4; Sec. 3.3.1, especially topology/embedding assumptions and the foliation-induced τ at lines 629–639; Sec. 3.4; Sec. 4.1; Sec. 5.1.2–5.1.5, especially equations (5.1.163)–(5.1.171).
assumptions: In the ADM treatment the review takes a compact three-manifold Σ for simplicity and assumes spacetime topology permits a one-parameter foliation by embeddings F_t:Σ→M, t∈R (Sec. 3.3.1); this is a setup assumption, not a consequence established there for arbitrary spacetimes. A foliation defines τ(F_t(x))=t, called physically artificial by the author (Sec. 3.3.1).
conclusion: The author presents Dirac quantization as imposing momentum and Hamiltonian constraints on physical states. In this treatment the Hamiltonian is a combination of constraints, yielding the frozen-formalism issue; the review also discusses internal-time alternatives and global-time/multiple-choice obstructions. Its foliation parameter is not an operational clock or a proof of a preferred physical time.
proof_status: Review, not a theorem paper; primary HTML read selectively through relevant sections, not cover-to-cover; no technical result independently audited.
dependencies: ADM and Kuchař works discussed/cited by the review
open_questions: How candidate internal clocks can be globally defined and yield equivalent quantum theories remains approach-dependent.
limits: The review’s compact-Σ/topologically foliable canonical setup narrows its scope. Statements about all quantum gravity approaches should not be inferred from this canonical discussion.

title: The Problem of Time in Quantum Gravity
version: arXiv 1009.2157v3 (20 Jul 2012 HTML revision); chapter version noted by arXiv as 2012
relevance: Multifaceted taxonomy of canonical quantum gravity’s problem of time, including foliation dependence, global time, internal York time, and quantum ambiguities.
locators: Sec. 1.2, frozen formalism and compact-without-boundary Σ convention; Sec. 1.4–1.5, facets; Sec. 2.4, York-time candidate and existence/constructibility problems; Sec. 1.5 around lines 131–133 for global-time separation issues.
assumptions: Review focuses substantially on canonical GR; footnote to Sec. 1 takes compact spatial topology without boundary for simplicity. Different strategies add different premises; York-time sections concern constant-mean-curvature approaches and their restricted existence/constructibility.
conclusion: Anderson argues the frozen Wheeler–DeWitt equation is one facet among several: classical and quantum foliation dependence, constraint closure, multiple choice, global-time and spacetime reconstruction issues. He reports that classical GR’s refoliation properties do not supply established quantum-level guarantees. This is a review taxonomy, not a no-time theorem.
proof_status: Review HTML read in selected sections; technical proofs and the entire review not audited.
dependencies: Isham and Kuchař reviews cited by Anderson
open_questions: Whether a particular quantization resolves these facets is formulation-specific; this review does not prove a general impossibility result.
limits: Partial reading. Do not treat the author’s classification or cited open difficulties as an established universal obstruction.
